choices.text: Logic identifies the facts; it does not rewrite them to protect a clash
Editing facts is fine, but only if the wording stays long
The only problem is that editing takes time
Contradictions are too rare to bother checking

feedback.note: Changing the report of the facts to save both sides of a contradiction abandons identification.

exercises.prompt: Match each discovery to the proper next step.

pairs.left: A later check removes the clash
pairs.right: The error in thinking has been corrected

pairs.left: Someone calls the clash a fact about reality

feedback.note: The proper next step is correction of the thinking. A contradiction is not left in place and renamed as reality.

exercises.prompt: Fill the contrast.

parts.text: The contradiction is an error in

feedback.note: Reality is what identification has to match. When identifications clash, the thinking is what must change.

exercises.prompt: What is the difference between arriving at a contradiction and maintaining one?

choices.text: Arriving exposes an error; maintaining keeps the error in place
They are the same act, and both are the goal of logic
Maintaining is better because it shows you can hold two ideas
Arriving blames the world, and maintaining corrects it

feedback.note: Finding the clash is the confession of an error. Keeping the clash is refusing to correct it.

exercises.prompt: Someone says both claims must stand even though they contradict. What has that person done with logic?

choices.text: Left the art of non-contradictory identification
Used logic in its strictest form
Finished the identification and stopped, correctly
Proved that the facts contradict themselves

feedback.note: To maintain a contradiction is to stop identifying without contradiction. That is an exit from logic, not a use of it.

exercises.prompt: Match each choice to its result.

pairs.left: Drop the claim that caused the clash
Notice the clash and recheck the facts
pairs.right: Use the contradiction as a warning

feedback.note: The warning is useful only if you then drop the error. Keeping both claims throws the warning away.

exercises.prompt: Complete the contrast.

parts.text: Arrive at a contradiction and you confess an error;
it and you refuse to correct that error.

feedback.note: Maintaining is the further step: the error is known, and it is kept anyway.

exercises.prompt: Build the sentence that says what maintaining a contradiction does.

feedback.note: There is no deeper truth in holding both sides. The hold itself is the failure of the art.

exercises.prompt: You discover that your conclusion contradicts a fact you already identified. Which step stays inside logic?

choices.text: Give up the conclusion or correct the earlier identification, whichever the facts require
Announce that both will be kept as a special case
Erase the fact so the conclusion can stay
Rename the clash so it no longer counts as a contradiction

feedback.note: Logic keeps the identifications that match the facts and drops the one that contradicts them. Renaming the clash does not remove it.

exercises.prompt: Why does keeping a known contradiction cut you off from the facts?

choices.text: You are no longer identifying one thing as what it is
The wording sounds less confident
Checking takes longer than asserting
Other people may disagree with your style

feedback.note: If both of two incompatible identifications stand, you have stopped saying what the thing is. Contact with that fact is what you give up.

exercises.prompt: Match each stage to the right name.

pairs.left: You first notice that two claims clash
You insist on both claims after you know they clash
You withdraw the claim that does not fit the facts

feedback.note: The three stages are not the same act. Only the third returns you to the art.

exercises.prompt: Build the closing rule of the unit.

feedback.note: That is the whole art in this unit: identify what is, and do not maintain a contradiction.

exercises.prompt: Which summary fits this unit and no wider topic?

choices.text: Logic is the art of non-contradictory identification
Logic is a replacement for the senses
Logic is a count of how many people agree
Logic is the mood that follows a conclusion

feedback.note: The unit is that art: identify, refuse the contradiction, and do not keep the clash once you see it.

exercises.prompt: In this unit, what is a context of knowledge?

choices.text: The facts and earlier ideas a claim depends on
The feeling you have while you say the claim
The number of people who repeat the claim
The wording you happen to prefer

feedback.note: Context is the knowledge the claim rests on. Mood, popularity, and style do not supply that base.

exercises.prompt: Why is knowledge called contextual?

choices.text: A claim holds in relation to the knowledge that supports it
A claim means whatever the speaker feels today
A claim needs no facts once it has a name
A claim is true only when a group agrees

feedback.note: Contextual means the claim is tied to a definite body of knowledge, not that truth is a feeling or a vote.

exercises.prompt: Match each item to its role in a context.

pairs.left: Earlier ideas the claim relies on
A mood that is not evidence

feedback.note: Facts and the ideas that depend on them form the context. A mood left unconnected to those facts does not.

exercises.prompt: Complete the lesson statement.

parts.text: : a claim depends on the facts and ideas already in hand.

feedback.note: The word for this dependence is contextual. Optional, private, and random deny that dependence.

exercises.prompt: Build the sentence that states what a context is.

feedback.note: Context names the supporting knowledge. It is not a substitute for the facts and it is not a mood.

exercises.prompt: You say the bridge is safe. Which item belongs in the context of that claim?

choices.text: The inspection results and the engineering ideas those results use
How much you hope the trip goes well
The fact that the bridge has a name
How confidently you say the word safe

feedback.note: The context is the knowledge the safety claim depends on. Hope, a label, and a tone of voice are not that knowledge.

exercises.prompt: Match each mistake to what it confuses with context.

pairs.left: My feeling makes the claim true
Everyone says it, so the base is done
The word itself is the whole proof

feedback.note: Context is supporting knowledge. A feeling, a chorus, or a word used alone does not do that job.

exercises.prompt: Finish the contrast.

parts.text: A claim is contextual when it stays tied to its

feedback.note: The tie that matters is to supporting knowledge, not to secrecy, popularity, or emotion.

exercises.prompt: What does hierarchical mean for knowledge?

choices.text: Later knowledge rests on earlier knowledge in a definite order
Every idea is equally basic and can be swapped at will
Ideas are ranked by how impressive they sound
The newest sentence always replaces the older facts

feedback.note: Hierarchy is an order of dependence. It is not a pile, a contest of tone, or a rule that the newest line wins.

exercises.prompt: Which use respects the hierarchy?

choices.text: You keep the earlier facts in place and then draw the later conclusion
You start with the later conclusion and deny the facts it needed
You treat a remote conclusion as if it were your first observation
You erase the earlier step because the later word sounds complete

feedback.note: The order runs from earlier knowledge to later knowledge. Skipping, swapping, or erasing the base breaks that order.

exercises.prompt: Match each item to its place in the order.

pairs.left: What you know first and directly
A conclusion that uses that earlier knowledge
A later conclusion used as if nothing came before it

feedback.note: Earlier knowledge supports later knowledge. Treating the later item as free-standing breaks the order.

exercises.prompt: Complete the unit line about order.

feedback.note: The dependence runs from earlier to later. Loudness, novelty, and vagueness are not the order.

exercises.prompt: Build the sentence that states the order.

feedback.note: Hierarchy means later knowledge rests on earlier knowledge. It does not cancel that base, and a vote is not the base.

exercises.prompt: Someone uses an advanced conclusion to wipe out the simple facts it was built from. What failed?

choices.text: The hierarchy: the later item was turned against the earlier base
Only the tone of voice
Only the speed of the sentence
Nothing, because later always outranks earlier

feedback.note: A later conclusion cannot erase the earlier knowledge it depends on. That reversal is a break in the hierarchy.

exercises.prompt: Match each move to the result.

pairs.left: Keep the earlier facts, then conclude
Treat every idea as equally first
Use a late conclusion to cancel its base

feedback.note: Keeping the base preserves the hierarchy. Flattening every idea, or reversing the dependence, does not.

exercises.prompt: Build the warning about order.

feedback.note: The warning is about place in the order. A slogan and a refusal of order are not the correction.

exercises.prompt: Which pair names the two features in this unit's title?

choices.text: Context and hierarchy
Mood and memory tricks
Polls and slogans
Style and volume

feedback.note: The unit is about context and hierarchy. Moods, polls, slogans, style, and volume are not those features.

exercises.prompt: When is a concept floating?

choices.text: When it is used with no context
When the word has many letters
When the idea was learned long ago
When more than one person knows the word

feedback.note: Floating means used with no context. Length, age, and how many people know the word are not the test.

exercises.prompt: What has a floating concept lost?

choices.text: Its tie to the facts and to the knowledge that comes before it
Its spelling, while the meaning stays fully specified
Its fans, while the context stays explicit
Nothing but the ink on the page

feedback.note: With no context, the concept is detached from the facts and from the earlier knowledge that give it meaning.

exercises.prompt: Match each use to floating or not floating.

pairs.left: A word waved with no facts and no earlier ideas attached
The same word tied to the facts it names and the ideas it rests on
A grand term used as if it needed no base at all

feedback.note: The difference is context. A tied concept is not floating. A word with no base is floating, however grand it sounds.

exercises.prompt: Complete the unit summary line.

parts.text: A concept used with no context is

feedback.note: No context means the concept is floating. Finished, forbidden, and automatic are different claims.

exercises.prompt: Build the sentence that names the fault.

feedback.note: Used with no context, the concept is floating. That is not the same as being grounded, and it does not mean meaning is unnecessary.

exercises.prompt: Which speaker is using a floating concept?

choices.text: Justice matters, and I will not say which facts or earlier ideas I mean
Justice here means this rule applied to these stated facts
This conclusion comes after the observations I just listed
I can point to the earlier knowledge this word rests on

feedback.note: Refusing to name any facts or earlier ideas leaves the concept with no context. The other speakers keep that tie.

exercises.prompt: Does a long explanation by itself stop a concept from floating?

choices.text: No. Length is not context. The tie to facts and to earlier knowledge is
Yes. Any long speech supplies a context automatically
Yes, if the speech uses bigger words than the question
Only when the speech is delivered loudly

feedback.note: A concept floats when context is missing. More words, bigger words, or more volume do not replace that context.

exercises.prompt: Fill both blanks.

parts.text: Floating means the concept is cut off from its

feedback.note: What is missing is context and the order of knowledge. Volume and costume are not those missing pieces.

exercises.prompt: Match the phrase to the idea it illustrates.

pairs.left: Tied to the knowledge it depends on
Placed after the knowledge it rests on

feedback.note: No context makes the concept float. A tie to supporting knowledge, and a place after that knowledge, keeps it from floating.

exercises.prompt: What is the first useful move when a concept is floating?

choices.text: Name the facts it refers to and the earlier knowledge it rests on
Repeat the word more forcefully
Swap in a fancier synonym and stop
Declare that context is impossible

feedback.note: Putting a concept back means restoring its context: the facts and the earlier knowledge. Force, a synonym, or a denial does not do that.

exercises.prompt: Which reply puts freedom back into a context?

choices.text: Here it means these people may take these actions, on the facts and rules already stated
Freedom is just a glow-word, and that is all I will say
Freedom means anything, so no facts are required
I will use the late political slogan to erase the earlier facts

feedback.note: The useful reply states referents and the knowledge already in place. A glow, a blank meaning, or a reversal of order leaves the concept floating.

exercises.prompt: Match each repair to what it restores.

pairs.left: Point to the facts the word refers to
Show which earlier knowledge the word rests on

feedback.note: Facts restore what the concept is about. Earlier knowledge restores its place. Emphasis restores neither.

exercises.prompt: Complete the repair.

parts.text: To stop a concept from floating, state its

feedback.note: The repair is to state the context. Volume, a slogan, or a synonym is not a substitute.

exercises.prompt: Build the sentence that says how to restore a concept.

feedback.note: Restoration names facts and earlier knowledge. Shouting a label does not put the concept back.

exercises.prompt: A student says the concept is too advanced to connect to anything earlier. What is wrong with that?

choices.text: It denies the hierarchy by treating a later concept as if it had no base
It proves the concept is fully in context
It shows that earlier knowledge is optional once a word is long
It fixes a floating concept by calling it advanced

feedback.note: Advanced does not mean baseless. A later concept still rests on earlier knowledge. Calling it advanced does not restore context.

exercises.prompt: Match the attempted fix to the verdict.

pairs.left: Specify the referents and the prior knowledge
Offer a synonym and no facts
Insist the later word cancels the earlier facts

feedback.note: Only the tie to referents and prior knowledge restores the concept. A synonym or a reversal leaves the fault in place.

exercises.prompt: Fill both blanks in the repair rule.

parts.text: the concept refers to and the

feedback.note: The two things to state are the facts and the earlier knowledge. Applause and font are irrelevant.

exercises.prompt: Which pair of questions checks this unit in one pass?

choices.text: What knowledge does this depend on, and is that knowledge earlier in the order?
How loud is the claim, and how new is the wording?
Who agrees, and who said it first in the room?
How does it feel, and does the word sound important?

feedback.note: The check is context plus hierarchy: the supporting knowledge, and its earlier place. Volume, novelty, agreement, and feeling are not the check.

exercises.prompt: A conclusion names real facts but treats those facts as less basic than itself. Which part failed?

choices.text: The hierarchy: the order of dependence is upside down
Nothing, because any mention of facts completes both checks
Only the spelling of the conclusion
Only the speaker's mood, which this unit treats as the context

feedback.note: Mentioning facts starts the context. Turning those facts into something less basic than the conclusion still breaks the hierarchy.

exercises.prompt: Match each case to the check it fails.

pairs.left: The word is used with no facts and no prior ideas
pairs.right: Fails context: the concept is floating

pairs.left: A later conclusion is used to erase its base
pairs.right: Fails hierarchy: the order is reversed

pairs.left: Facts are named and the conclusion comes after them

feedback.note: No context leaves the concept floating. A reversed order breaks the hierarchy. Named facts followed by the conclusion pass both.

exercises.prompt: Complete the summary.

feedback.note: The two words that belong together here are contextual and hierarchical. The other bank words drop one or both.

exercises.prompt: Build the full summary sentence.

tokens.text: and a concept with no context is floating

feedback.note: The unit summary joins both features, then names the floating concept. Mood and the denial of order are the errors the summary rejects.

exercises.prompt: You can state the context, and that context is earlier than the conclusion. What should you say about the concept?

choices.text: It is held in context and in the hierarchy
It is floating because a check was even needed
It is floating because the context came first
It is floating until a crowd approves the wording

feedback.note: A stated context that is earlier than the conclusion is exactly the hold this unit asks for. Needing the check, or having the base first, is not a fault.

exercises.prompt: Which statement keeps both ideas without turning either into the other?

choices.text: Context is the supporting knowledge. Hierarchy is the order of that support. A concept with neither tie is floating
Context and hierarchy are the same word, so one question is enough
Hierarchy replaces context, so facts need not be named
Context replaces hierarchy, so a later idea may come first

feedback.note: Context answers what the claim depends on. Hierarchy answers the order of that dependence. Dropping either one leaves the concept unanchored.

exercises.prompt: Fill both blanks in the closing check.

feedback.note: The two-part check asks for the context and for its earlier place. Louder and newer are not the standard.

exercises.prompt: Match each unit idea to the short test.

pairs.right: The claim depends on definite knowledge
That knowledge comes earlier in the order
The concept is used with no context

feedback.note: Contextual names the dependence, hierarchical names the order, and floating names a concept used with no context.

exercises.prompt: Build the closing reminder.

feedback.note: The reminder holds both requirements at once. A slogan, or a concept placed ahead of every fact, drops them.
